vignette:
The Weight of Numbers

Karim is twenty-two years old, recently hired at an accounting firm where he spends his days moving through columns of figures, searching for discrepancies that others have missed. He is good at his work - methodical, precise, the kind of person who notices when something is off by a single digit. His colleagues describe him as quiet and professional. What they do not know is that he arrives at the office each morning having slept perhaps three hours, and that he has memorized every exit in the building.

Fourteen months ago, Karim was sexually assaulted by a man he had met through mutual friends at a gathering after work. He had not been drinking heavily. He had not done anything wrong. These are facts he has repeated to himself so many times that they have begun to feel like a script rather than a truth he actually believes. The assault happened in an apartment not far from where he now lives, and there are three streets he will not walk down because they pass too close to that building.

In the weeks that followed, Karim told no one. He comes from a family where men are expected to be composed and strong, and where the subject of sexual violence - particularly when the victim is male - exists in a kind of cultural silence so complete that he could not find words for what had happened even when he was alone with his own thoughts. He showered compulsively for the first month. He stopped eating regular meals. He applied for the auditing position during this period almost on autopilot, and when he got the job he felt nothing - not pride, not relief, only a faint sense that the world was continuing to move around him while he stood somewhere slightly outside of it.

Now, more than a year later, Karim sits at his desk and loses stretches of time. He will be reviewing a financial statement and then suddenly he is back in that room, not remembering it so much as reliving it - the smell, the weight, the helplessness - and when he surfaces he finds that twenty minutes have passed and his hands are pressed flat against the desk as though he is trying to hold himself down. He has learned to schedule his most demanding work for the mornings, when he is least likely to be ambushed by his own mind.

He startles badly when colleagues approach from behind, and has rearranged his workstation so that his back faces the wall. He has declined every after-work invitation for over a year, offering excuses about early mornings and project deadlines. Socializing feels not merely unpleasant but genuinely unsafe - his body reads proximity to unfamiliar men as threat, and the effort of managing that response for an entire evening leaves him exhausted in a way that regular tiredness does not.

Karim sleeps poorly and dreams vividly, waking with his heart slamming and a shame so acute it feels physical, like something pressing on his sternum. He has begun to believe, in the quiet logic of three in the morning, that the assault revealed something true and shameful about him - that it happened because of who he is, some weakness or wrongness that the right person could simply see. He knows, in the daylight, that this is not rational. But knowing and believing are not the same thing, and the distance between them has become one of the defining features of his life.

He is, by most external measures, functioning. He meets his deadlines. He calls his mother on Sundays. He keeps his apartment clean. But there is a flatness to his days that he struggles to name - a sense that the person he was before the assault was someone he knew well, and the person he is now is someone he is still trying to understand. He came to therapy not because he felt ready, but because he had run out of ways to manage alone.
